title: Spray and pray outbound doesn't work anymore ... What now? - With Diana Ross
speakers_and_attribution: Adam Robinson is the primary host; Diana Ross is the principal guest and an operator moving from retention.com to RB2B. Santosh, whose surname is not supplied, co-hosts and asks several questions. Audience guests include Sam of Assign AI and Barath Sundararaman of TraceLink; names follow the automatic captions and are not independently verified. The captions are not diarized, so speaker assignments use conversational context. Most sales methods and career stories are Diana's statements, even when they concern Adam's companies. Captions variously render RB2B as RV2B, Our B2B and our B2B; those references are interpreted contextually as RB2B.
summary: The discussion covers building an early sales process, learning and revisiting ICP, operating with simple tools, hiring for the right stage, and adapting outbound as a company and its market change. Diana emphasizes customer conversations, consistent activity, manual prospect selection, short sales presentations, weekly review and restrained email follow-up. She explicitly lacks a validated new outbound playbook for RB2B and plans to begin with unconverted trial users. Adam contributes concrete reflections on retention.com's CRM-free growth, changing publisher strategy, enterprise credibility, RB2B's expectation and churn problems, and mistakes in early sales hiring. The title overstates the certainty of the discussion: the speakers see continued outbound opportunity, while distinguishing historical successes, current practices and untested ideas.

key_learnings.claim: Diana's prerequisites for a lean sales operation are a good product, a working hypothesis about its buyer, basic sales visibility and a credible-looking website. The ICP should evolve as conversations reveal who buys and why.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: These are Diana's operating principles. She explicitly says RB2B's precise ICP was still unresolved.

key_learnings.claim: Internal engineering support can make a small sales team more effective by exposing new signups, account size, opportunities and sales results. Adam clarifies that the CTO's contribution here was internal dashboards rather than customer-facing features.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross, with clarification from Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: The workflow is described by Diana; no measured productivity improvement is supplied. The CTO's name is captioned as Tate.

key_learnings.claim: Outbound provides control over whom to approach and which message to test; inbound can reveal valuable segments outside the planned prospect list and often closes faster. Diana recommends learning from both rather than treating them as mutually exclusive.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: Based on her experience with GetEmails/retention.com and earlier sales work. Her claim that new businesses start without inbound is a generalization.

key_learnings.claim: Consistent, appropriate sales activity matters even when results lag. Diana uses lessons from Xerox to sustain effort through rejection, while acknowledging that the activities themselves must be the right ones.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: Her assertion that salespeople will not have three bad days is a motivational maxim, not a demonstrated guarantee.

key_learnings.claim: Early sales benefits from entrepreneurial curiosity: understand a customer's business, keep revising the process and feed new objections or competitor information back to the founder. Diana describes calling Adam after sales conversations to discuss what she learned.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: Diana reports the collaboration; this does not independently establish an Adam-wide management philosophy.

key_learnings.claim: Review sales weekly and examine calendar use, outbound activity, inbound conversations and closing progress. Diana considers monthly or quarterly review too slow for early iteration and supplements reporting with judgment about conversation quality.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: Her process mixes data and gut feel; she does not provide a controlled decision framework or numerical pivot threshold.

key_learnings.claim: Adam sees retention.com's growth without a CRM as evidence that early sales fundamentals matter more than accumulating tools. The company used a Google Sheet until the reported $10 million ARR milestone.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: A retrospective example from this company, not evidence that CRMs are universally unnecessary.

key_learnings.claim: Diana used a color-coded sheet to keep important opportunities visible and prioritize follow-up with little administrative overhead. She continued using a personal sheet even when a CRM existed and had just created one for RB2B.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: She says the sheet could be messy and hard for other people to understand; it is not presented as a scalable shared system.

key_learnings.claim: Diana is open to AI that increases her productive activity but had not begun using AI in sales and did not then plan to hire AI SDRs. Her stated preference is assistance with her work rather than immediate replacement of her selling role.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: A provisional position at the time of the recording. She explicitly leaves room to try AI SDRs and says she is still learning.

key_learnings.claim: ICP discovery should include actual selling: start with a buyer hypothesis, reflect on conversations, deliver a pitch and price, and observe whether people buy. Repeated conversations without a purchase test can conceal weak fit.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: Her advice to present confidently is not evidence that a product has capabilities it lacks. She provides no statistically defined sample size.

key_learnings.claim: A short presentation helped GetEmails explain the product, common objections and pricing consistently. Diana came to view that education as an indicator of whether customers would use the product successfully.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross, with corroborating recollection from Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: The impact is qualitative. Adam remembers six slides; Diana remembers five.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says RB2B's product-led motion was setting incorrect expectations about what the product should do and where its value lay. His own view of the value had changed, and he sees a sales presentation as a way to align expectations with what the company can deliver.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: He does not specify the old or new value proposition in this passage. He says this is his and Diana's first PLG experience, while distinguishing Santosh's prior experience.

key_learnings.claim: Before adding a salesperson at RB2B, Diana wants to work the calls herself until she can see a repeatable process. She also believes doing the job personally builds credibility with the eventual team.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: Her proposed month of hands-on work is a plan, not a proven hiring threshold. A brief interjection suggests it could take two or three months.

key_learnings.claim: Adam distinguishes the founder-like ability to invent the first sales process from the ability to execute an established process with strong negotiation and CRM skills. He advises hiring people with experience at the company's actual stage.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: He allows that one person may span multiple stages. His first 100, next 1,000 and subsequent 5,000 demos are illustrative stages, not reported company volumes.

key_learnings.claim: Barath favors finding a few customers, delivering strong outcomes and expanding from that base before broad messaging or chasing every deal. He describes this as an unresolved challenge for TraceLink's young supply-chain business.
key_learnings.speaker: Barath Sundararaman
key_learnings.caveat: This is an audience guest's strategy and challenge, not Adam's company history or an established outcome.

key_learnings.claim: Diana reports that manual outreach outperformed automated campaigns in tests she ran around 2017. A Philippines-based manual-email operation then worked for several years, but she explicitly separates that historical playbook from what she still needs to test now.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: No response-rate or revenue comparison is provided. The company and dates for every part of the historical operation are not unambiguously established.

key_learnings.claim: Retention.com's pipeline strategy changed as its brand matured: agency and affiliate partnerships performed well for a period, and targeted in-person events became a current tactic. Diana says a hosted Taylor Swift concert created valuable face-to-face access to selected accounts.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: No event cost, pipeline or closed-revenue result is supplied. She explicitly says this kind of event is unsuitable at approximately $1 million ARR.

key_learnings.claim: Diana prioritizes carefully selected prospects over generic database exports. She worries that common filters produce the same over-contacted lists and that employee records can be stale; her preference is to begin with LinkedIn and hand-pick companies.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: Her belief that LinkedIn is the most current source is not independently verified. She acknowledges data providers can work and that enrichment has become easier.

key_learnings.claim: Diana doubts that her former high-volume automated-email approach remains viable and dislikes alternate sending domains that weaken brand credibility. She presents these as observations and preferences while planning further tests.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: This is not a demonstrated universal failure of automation or domain rotation, and she provides no current comparative results.

key_learnings.claim: Diana believes the need to learn and prove a sales process applies to both bootstrapped and venture-backed companies. She recalls an unnamed situation where capital enabled hiring 25 salespeople before the process existed, which she describes as disastrous.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: She says her experience is primarily with bootstrapped companies. The funded situation's company, financing type, date and measured outcome are not identified.

key_learnings.claim: Diana's first RB2B sales priority is to revisit companies that tried the product but did not convert, because its existing inbound funnel gives her lower-funnel opportunities before new prospecting experiments.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: An intended priority just after joining, not a completed conversion improvement. She says it is not applicable to every startup.

key_learnings.claim: Technology purchases can indicate budget and a buyer's willingness to adopt new approaches. Diana previously targeted e-commerce companies using SMS tools for identity technology and wants to find analogous RB2B signals and promising verticals among existing users.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: The historical targeting logic is self-reported; RB2B indicators and tests were not yet defined or validated.

key_learnings.claim: Diana says she and Adam have often changed ICP through judgments formed in conversations rather than formal numerical thresholds. Her practical test is to make the pitch, state the price and observe the buyer's response.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: This is Diana's characterization of their joint decision-making. Her example counts of calls and outcomes are hypothetical.

key_learnings.claim: Adam describes retention.com's ICP as reversible rather than permanently settled: publishers were once large customers but had slow payments and sales cycles; the team focused on large Shopify stores, then returned to publishers with another offering and a newly closed contract.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This is a compressed retrospective without precise transition dates. The return also involved something else to sell, not simply a reversal under identical conditions.

key_learnings.claim: Adam interprets RB2B's churn as clear evidence that the current product is not a good fit for the current ICP.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: No churn percentage, cohort, period or distinction between logo and revenue churn is provided.

key_learnings.claim: Diana says publisher demand changed because the market's pain became more urgent. A segment that previously had other priorities appeared much more receptive to identity technology during the preceding six months.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: A qualitative observation about conversations, not a verified market-wide trend or measured adoption rate.

key_learnings.claim: Adam says brand presentation and customer proof eventually enabled retention.com to sell sophisticated enterprise products that a publisher had previously refused to buy from GetEmails. He advocates moving upmarket because he believes larger customers churn less and can sometimes be easier to sell to.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: The brand-credibility example is his self-report; the upmarket advice is a generalization with no comparative churn data here.

key_learnings.claim: Diana encourages startups to pursue larger brands that want an early advantage. She says an unnamed early customer's story became recurring proof that helped close other deals.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: The customer and resulting deal count or revenue are not supplied; the anecdote does not establish that all enterprises welcome startups.

key_learnings.claim: Diana supports automation for research and enrichment: retention.com uses Clay to inspect event lists, technology stacks, contacts and web traffic, and she likes combining BuiltWith lists with contact waterfalls. Her objection to automation does not extend to all sales tooling.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: She says she does not use Clay's AI and is less certain about the CRM/demo-form enrichment implementation.

key_learnings.claim: Diana's preferred sequence is a clear introduction with relevant customer proof and a question, a brief follow-up, a more specific explanation or case study, and sometimes a final recap after a longer pause. She keeps messages in one thread and favors three or four concise, personable emails.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross
key_learnings.caveat: A practitioner preference rather than an experimentally established optimum. She questions reusing familiar follow-up phrasing and balances persistence with avoiding excessive contact.

key_learnings.claim: Diana plans to publish more about her RB2B experiments, including what works, what fails and her views on AI sales tools. Adam welcomes that content while openly acknowledging the company's recent difficulty.
key_learnings.speaker: Diana Ross, followed by Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: Diana's content plan is prospective; it is not proof that those posts or experiments were subsequently published.

key_learnings.claim: Adam ends by emphasizing signal stacking as an important subject for contemporary outbound and announces a future session on it.
key_learnings.speaker: Adam Robinson
key_learnings.caveat: This is a brief endorsement and event preview. The transcript does not teach a signal-stacking method or establish its results.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam describes Diana as a valued business partner through repeated difficult and successful periods and says he wants to keep working with her for decades.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: Supports a specific statement about this working relationship, not a generalized or approved personal mission.

backstory_and_values.claim: Diana traces her sales discipline to selling photocopiers, making in-person calls in Canadian winters and receiving Xerox mentorship. She says this made working remotely in her first SaaS sales role at Maropost feel comparatively straightforward.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Diana Ross
backstory_and_values.caveat: Diana's career history, not Adam's. The sequence around 2014–2015 and starting her own business is imprecise.

backstory_and_values.claim: Diana says she ran a volleyball-training business after university and built an app at age 20. She identifies herself as an entrepreneur whose strength is sales and describes curiosity about customers as intrinsically motivating.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Diana Ross
backstory_and_values.caveat: Guest self-report; no company name, app details or commercial outcomes are given.

backstory_and_values.claim: Sam says he started Assign AI after struggling to automate commercial-property workflows in software without open APIs. He reports investing all the money he made in real estate because he wanted small-business owners to automate without specialist help.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Sam
backstory_and_values.caveat: An audience guest's origin and funding story, not Adam's. No investment amount or independent verification is supplied.

backstory_and_values.claim: Sam says Assign AI's available first version learns from screen recordings, but users still find it complicated. The team is therefore developing a conversational second version.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Sam
backstory_and_values.caveat: His earlier description sounds like conversational automation is available; this later clarification distinguishes the usable version from ongoing development.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam explicitly acknowledges having made a hiring mistake in his career around the specialized skills required to invent an initial sales process.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: He does not identify the company, hire, date or financial consequence.

backstory_and_values.claim: Diana describes moving from higher-level responsibility at retention.com back into hands-on sales at RB2B as an exciting opportunity to learn what has changed.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Diana Ross
backstory_and_values.caveat: Her exact titles and ongoing responsibilities across the two companies are not established.

backstory_and_values.claim: Adam publicly acknowledges that RB2B had become abruptly stuck and expresses confidence that work the team had not yet done could improve its value. He hopes the required package can be delivered over weeks or months.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Adam Robinson
backstory_and_values.caveat: The problem's scale and cause are not quantified; recovery and timing are expectations, not achieved results.

backstory_and_values.claim: Diana values persistence that remains personable and recalls a customer's positive feedback about her follow-up style. She also describes optimism as necessary for her work in sales.
backstory_and_values.speaker: Diana Ross
backstory_and_values.caveat: Two related statements within this interval; these are Diana's self-described values, not Adam's approved voice or identity.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam and Diana place their working relationship at approximately six years; Diana says they met around the holidays and were approaching that anniversary.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson and Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Approximate joint recollection relative to the recording. Publication does not establish an exact meeting date.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Assign AI's stated price was $3 per day at the time of the conversation.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Sam
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Guest-reported pricing, not revenue or customer traction. Currency and billing details are not specified.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Sam claims Assign AI was built by a team that had done substantial work on SpaceX and OpenAI.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Sam
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Unverified guest social proof; no names, employment relationships or project details are provided. It is not an endorsement by either organization.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Adam initially credits Diana as the only sales rep on two zero-to-$10 million journeys, then narrows the claim to two $1 million-to-$10 million journeys. Diana agrees with the narrowed version.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: The passage does not explicitly specify ARR, dates or name both businesses. Nearby discussion suggests Maropost and GetEmails/retention.com. One sales rep is not one total employee and does not exclude engineering, support or prospecting assistance.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Diana's photocopier-sales activity standards included 50 cold calls before leaving the office on Monday morning and 25 in-person cold calls each day.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical guest-reported job expectations, not Adam/company metrics. The wording should not be converted into 50 phone calls every day.

metrics_and_dates.claim: Diana places an early business/career transition around 2014–2015 and separately says she built an app at age 20.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: The two statements occur at 13:07–13:18 and 16:50–16:55. They do not establish a birth year or exact chronology.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Reported product-policy change as of the recording; no implementation date or conversion result is supplied.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical company milestone with no event date. ARR is not recognized annual revenue, profit or cash.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Approximate recollection about Diana's post, with no publication date or analytics evidence; these are not Adam's personal engagement metrics.

metrics_and_dates.claim: The early GetEmails presentation is remembered as six slides by Adam and five slides by Diana; Diana says it replaced a roughly 15-minute phone pitch.
metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson and Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Conflicting retrospective slide counts should be preserved. Neither speaker quantifies conversion lift.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross; interjecting host not certain
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Prospective staffing timeline, not an achieved hiring date. The interjection's speaker is uncertain.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Context maps the larger sales-led business to retention.com and the $4 million PLG business to RB2B, but this sentence does not name them. These are latest-in-conversation self-reported ARR figures, not audited revenue, profit or cash.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical guest report without a quantified performance difference or a fully specified company/date range.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Approximate historical figures. Headcount, employment versus contracting, overhead and exact company attribution are unstated; this is not a complete acquisition-cost calculation.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Relative event timing only. Attendance, spend, pipeline and revenue outcomes are not reported.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Historical personal activity figures without exact dates or company attribution; neither is presented as her current RB2B practice.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Approximate historical timing, with no prospect count, conversion rate or revenue result.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson
metrics_and_dates.caveat: A reported closed deal near the recording date, not recognized revenue or collected cash. Customer identity, commencement date and contract conditions are unstated.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Relative, approximate observation windows; no market-wide adoption metric is supplied.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Diana Ross
metrics_and_dates.caveat: Suggested cadence, not an achieved performance metric or universal optimum.

metrics_and_dates.speaker: Adam Robinson

tensions_and_corrections: The title implies a settled conclusion about outbound failure. Diana instead says outbound remains possible, her old methods are historical, and she needs further hands-on testing before offering a current early-stage playbook.
Adam corrects his own description of Diana from two zero-to-$10 million journeys as sole rep to two $1 million-to-$10 million journeys. The initial version should not become an unqualified wiki fact.

A sole sales rep is not a sole employee: the conversation describes CTO-built dashboards, support collaboration and a separate manual outreach operation. No complete FTE, contractor or shared-support ledger is available.
Adam recalls a six-slide GetEmails presentation; Diana recalls five. Preserve the discrepancy rather than choosing one.
Sam initially describes chat-based automation, then clarifies that the usable first version requires screen recording and the conversational second version is under development.

Diana's resistance to automated sending and generic lists coexists with her use of Clay, BuiltWith, contact waterfalls and enrichment. Her position is selective, not anti-tool or anti-automation in general.
Diana advocates consistent activity but also continuous iteration. Her advice does not support repeating an ineffective ICP, message or process indefinitely.
Weekly reporting and dashboards coexist with gut-based ICP decisions. No universal conversion threshold or minimum sample size is established.
Retention.com's return to publishers followed changes in market pain, brand credibility and what it could sell. It is not evidence that the earlier Shopify focus was simply mistaken.

Adam's view of RB2B's value proposition had changed, and he links current churn to poor product/ICP fit. Neither the revised value proposition nor a quantified churn analysis appears in the transcript.
Diana's proposed hiring delay, AI exploration, RB2B tests and public posting are plans. The transcript supplies no subsequent outcomes.
Premium hosted events are described as effective at retention.com's current stage, with an explicit warning that this approach is not suitable at roughly $1 million ARR.

Diana says she has primarily worked in bootstrapped settings while recounting a capital-enabled hiring failure. The unnamed case should not be labeled venture-backed or attributed to Adam without further evidence.
Publication time is known; recording time is not. References to yesterday, the last seven days, a couple of weeks ago and the next month should remain relative.
TraceLink's guest claims market leadership and unusually severe US drug shortages in the current year, but supplies no supporting data. These are unverified guest statements, not Adam/company proof.
